cards.title: 400: invalid tool schema
cards.body: Strict schemas need additionalProperties: false and every field required. Use schema_for().

cards.title: 400: missing tool_result
cards.body: Every tool_use needs a tool_result with its id, all in the next user message.

cards.title: The model picks the wrong tool
cards.body: Improve the descriptions: what, when, returns, rules. Remove overlapping tools.

cards.title: The agent seems stuck
cards.body: A tool has no timeout, or it's too long. Every tool gets one.

items.q: Walk me through what happens when an agent calls a tool.
items.a: Your code sends tools + messages. The model replies `stop_reason: tool_use` with `tool_use` blocks. Your code **validates**, **checks permission**, **runs with a timeout**, and returns `tool_result`s (same ids, `is_error` on failure) in one user message. Repeat until no tool calls.
items.trap: Skipping validation and permissions, or saying the API runs the tool.

items.q: How would you let an agent send emails safely?
items.a: Make `send_email` a **danger** tool: validate recipients and content, show the human the exact email and ask for approval **every time**, log decisions, rate-limit, and start in a read-only or draft-only mode.
items.trap: "Add 'never send spam' to the system prompt." Instructions are not enforcement.

items.q: What's the difference between strict tool use and validating in your code?
items.a: Strict tool use guarantees the input **matches the schema**: fields and types. Your validation enforces **limits and business rules**, and turns failures into clear errors the model can fix.
items.trap: Treating them as alternatives. You want both.

items.text: Tools: the model requests, your code runs, results return by id
A registry and Pydantic: one source of truth for every tool
Parallel calls: run them all, one message of results
Validate every input; give every tool a timeout
Least privilege, permission levels, and a human yes for danger

scenes.question: Who actually runs a tool's function?
options: The Claude API, on its servers
Your code, after the model requests it
The model, inside its reply
The Anthropic SDK, automatically, in every case
scenes.explain: The model only requests a call with a tool_use block. Your code decides whether and how to run it.

scenes.question: Why generate tool schemas from Pydantic classes?
options: Pydantic schemas are shorter
One class both describes the input to the model and validates it in code
The API only accepts Pydantic
It makes the model faster
scenes.explain: One source of truth: the schema the model sees and the validation your code runs come from the same class.

scenes.question: With strict: true, which check is still your job?
options: That required fields are present
That the priority is one of the enum values
That the task with that id exists
That no extra fields are sent
scenes.explain: Strict mode guarantees shape and types. Only your code knows which tasks exist, and other business rules.

scenes.question: A thread timeout fires after 2 seconds. What does it guarantee?
options: The tool's work is undone
The agent stops waiting and gets an error result
The thread is killed
The tool is retried automatically
scenes.explain: It stops the waiting, not the work. Use a process when you must be able to stop the work.

scenes.question: Where must the human-approval check for delete_task live?
options: In the system prompt
In the tool description
In your code, between validation and execution
In the model's reply to the user
scenes.explain: Only code enforces. Prompts and descriptions guide the model, but can't stop a call.

captions.text: Welcome back.
The store, the tools and the policy are ready.
Now we connect them in the agent loop, run a full demo, break things on purpose, and
look at the tests.
Then we'll wrap up the module with interview questions, a quiz, and your extension
challenge.
First, the system prompt.
Notice the style from Module 3: it explains why, not just what.
The tools are the only way to read or change the data, so the model has a reason to
use them.
It asks for parallel tool calls when the user wants several independent things.
And it says how to behave: look up a task's number first, fix the input after an
error, and never retry an action the user declined.
Today's date is filled in, so the model can write due dates correctly.
Act runs one tool call through run tool, with the policy.
Any tool error, invalid input, a denied action, a timeout, becomes a step marked as
an error.
Never a crash.
Run is the loop you know from Module 4: a step limit, a budget check, and clean
stops for a refusal or a cut-off reply.
No tool calls means the model has answered.
And here's what's new.
We act on every tool call in the reply, in order, report each step to the trace, and
collect the results.
Then all the results go back in one single user message, exactly as lesson two
showed.
Now a full demo, from an empty store.
First, reset.
Three tasks in one request.
One turn with three parallel calls, and each task gets its number.
Complete task three, and save a note, again in one turn.
And two read tools together: all tasks, with buy milk marked done, and the note we
just saved.
Now the safety features, on purpose.
Delete task one: the agent asks, with the task's title and due date.
The answer is no, so pay rent stays.
Delete task two, and this time the answer is yes, so it's deleted.
In read-only mode, writes are blocked.
And a rejected API key ends with one clear line, and exit code one.
No traceback anywhere.
The tests run the real loop, the real tools and the real policy, against the fake
model, with a temporary data file.
This one checks parallel calls: three steps, all in turn one, and the results
matched to the calls by ID, in one message.
This one checks recovery from invalid input: first an error step, then a successful
one, and exactly one task saved.
And these check the human approval: when the answer is no, the task is still there,
and the policy logged declined.
When it's yes, the task is gone.
Forty-three tests, all passing, with no key, no network, and without touching your
real data file.
And mypy is happy with every type hint.
A four hundred about the tool schema usually means a strict schema rule: additional
properties must be false, and every field required.
Generate schemas with schema for, instead of by hand.
A four hundred about tool use IDs means a result is missing.
Every call needs its result, all in the next user message.
If the model picks the wrong tool, improve the descriptions, and remove tools that
overlap.
And if the agent seems stuck, a tool probably has no timeout.
Every tool gets one.

Your code sends the tools and the messages.

Your code validates each input, checks the permission, runs it with a timeout, and

Then repeat until there are no tool calls.
The trap: skipping validation and permissions, or saying the API runs the tool.
Question two, a scenario: how would you let an agent send emails safely?
Make send email a danger tool.
Validate the recipients and the content.
Show the human the exact email, and ask for approval every time.
Log every decision, limit how many it can send, and start with a draft-only mode.

And question three: what's the difference between strict tool use and validating in

Strict tool use guarantees the input matches the schema: the fields and the types.
Your validation enforces limits and business rules, and turns failures into clear
errors the model can fix.
The trap: treating them as alternatives.
You want both.

With tools, the model requests, your code runs, and the results come back by ID.
A registry and Pydantic give one source of truth for every tool.
For parallel calls, run them all, and send one message of results.
Validate every input, and give every tool a timeout.
And use least privilege, permission levels, and a human yes for anything dangerous.
